title: The merchant and the parrot
hook: a caged parrot asks its merchant to greet the wild parrots of India (Masnavi 1.1547ff)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daimon: Marcus told himself to stand upright, not propped up. Did you say the honest thing? Day one hundred eighty-four, the last day of the week.

Somebody you love is going somewhere you can't. A cousin flying back to the country your family came from. A friend going home to the town you both grew up in. And you say, without thinking: say hi to everyone for me. Tell them I miss them. It's a small line, but it carries a lot. It says: part of me belongs there. Rumi's next story starts with that exact request. A rich merchant is getting ready for a long trip to India, and before he goes, he makes the rounds of his household. Today, the merchant and the parrot.
screen: `SAY HI TO EVERYONE FOR ME.` → `A MERCHANT BOUND FOR INDIA.` → `THE MERCHANT AND THE PARROT.`

segments.voice: The merchant is generous. He asks every servant and every member of the household: what shall I bring you from India? Each one names something. And then he comes to his parrot. It's a beautiful bird, and a clever one, and it lives in a cage in his house. What gift do you want? The parrot asks for no gift at all. It asks for a message to be carried. When you see the parrots of India, it says, flying free in the forests, give them my greeting. Tell them a parrot who longs for them is shut in a cage in my house, by the turning of fate. Ask them: is it right that I waste away here while you fly among the trees? Is this what friends do? Remember me, it says, when you're in the meadows at dawn. That's the whole request. Greet them for me. Rumi stops the story here for long reflections, and Sufi readers take the caged parrot as the human soul, kept in the cage of the body and this world, and the wild parrots as the saints, the friends of God, who are already free. That message is the soul's longing, sent home. You can hear the reed from earlier in this camp again: cut from the reedbed, and crying for it. Now look back at the week. In Rumi's story, the lion argued for tying the camel, a hare walked slowly on purpose, and the lion drowned fighting his own face, while Rumi pointed to the lion inside. In Marcus's notebook, cracked bread had its own beauty, and a person could stand upright, not propped. Two books, kept apart, and the week ends with a small caged bird asking only to be remembered. Tomorrow, his message arrives in India, and something happens nobody expected.
screen: `WHAT SHALL I BRING YOU FROM INDIA?` · `THE PARROT ASKS FOR A MESSAGE.` · `IS IT RIGHT I'M CAGED, YOU FREE?` · `THE SOUL, AND THE FREE FRIENDS.` · then, large: `GREET THEM FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: send a message to someone far. Settle, and breathe. Let someone come to mind who's far away: across the country, across an ocean, or just across a silence that's grown too long. What would you want them to hear? Not news. Just: I remember you. I miss you. I'm still here. Hold those words for a minute. Then, if you can, actually send it after the bell. The bell holds the time.
Masnavi, Rumi's book of stories: a caged parrot asks for no gift, only that its master greet the free parrots of India for it. Today's word.
Your line: greet them for me. Today, send the words you held, even one line, to someone far away. Day one hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: The merchant and the parrot is a story from the Masnavi's first book; Sufi teachers read the caged parrot as the soul and the parrots of India as the free friends of God.
